whatThisIs: The nakṣatra-vanaspati (Skt. nakṣatra-vṛkṣa) is ONE tree assigned to ONE lunar mansion, twenty-seven in a fixed order from Aśvinī. Monier-Williams glosses nakṣatra-vṛkṣa as a tree consecrated to a nakṣatra (MW-1); Böhtlingk's shorter Wörterbuch gives the same (MW-2). It is NOT the samidha (homa fuel) list and it is NOT a dhūpa (incense) list, and this ledger carries direct textual evidence that those are separately indexed categories. (a) SAMIDHA: Atharvaveda-Pariśiṣṭa 26 is the pariśiṣṭa devoted specifically to samidhs (AVP-6); its series — arka, palāśa, madhuka, nyagrodha, udumbara, plakṣa, aśvattha, then gomaya and kuśa, nine members (AVP-7) — is indexed by the text's own next words to the GRAHAS beginning with the Sun, not to the nakṣatras (AVP-8); and the same pariśiṣṭa gives a third, wholly different indexing principle, samidh chosen by PURPOSE — puṣṭi, śānti, wealth, kingship (AVP-9). (b) NAKṢATRA-INDEXED PLANT MATTER THAT IS NOT THIS LIST: Atharvaveda-Pariśiṣṭa 1, the Nakṣatrakalpa (AVP-1), runs a nakṣatra series at chs. 42–45 that is a BATHING rite (nakṣatra-snāna, AVP-2), and its cells are plural and heterogeneous — Kṛttikā takes a leaf-infusion of three trees at once (AVP-3), Ārdrā takes resins and aromatics rather than a tree (AVP-4), and Śraviṣṭhā/Dhaniṣṭhā takes sandalwood (AVP-5) where the tree list gives śamī. A nakṣatra-indexed plant is therefore not automatically a nakṣatra-vṛkṣa. (c) THE MERGE IS DOCUMENTED IN THE PRESENT TENSE, NOT IN THE TEXTS: a commercial devotional supplier sells a product called 'Nakshatra Samidha' and defines it on the page as the woods of the trees representing the 27 nakṣatras, for use in homa (BHAKTI-1, BHAKTI-2). That is category (1) sold as category (2). (d) AND ONE HONEST QUALIFICATION, because the tidy separation is not the whole evidence: the Nārada Purāṇa itself uses a person's janma-nakṣatra tree as homa fuel, three times in one chapter (NARP-5, NARP-6, NARP-7). So a textual bridge from the tree list to fire-fuel does exist — but it is specific (the wood is taken from an individual's birth star, not from a graha index) and it sits inside a hostile-rite (abhicāra) chapter. It is not the generic commercial 'nakṣatra samidha'. The two facts are kept side by side rather than resolved. FINALLY, on register: this is a living practice — plantings of nakṣatra groves are current (WIKI-1; SONI-7) — and the site records what named texts say, claims no efficacy of any kind, and carries no quantity and no process parameter.
earliestTextCarryingTheList: TWO witnesses carry the full 27, and THIS LEDGER DOES NOT ESTABLISH WHICH IS EARLIER. (1) Rājanighaṇṭu (Narahari), varga 2, vv. 2.41–2.46 in the GRETIL text of the Calcutta 1933 edition = vv. 33–38 in the Ānandāśrama Sanskrit Series no. 33, 1896, where the passage is a printed, titled section headed 'Nakṣatravṛkṣāḥ' (ANAND-1). It is the only witness that presents the list as an explicit doctrinal section, announces it ('now I shall state the nakṣatra trees, known from scripture' — RAJNI-1 = ANAND-2), states its own count and indexing rule ('these 27 trees have the nakṣatras as their deities, in order from Aśvinī; this is the nakṣatra-paddhati' — RAJNI-4), and names its own sources (RAJNI-6 = ANAND-11). It is also the only locus the 19th-century lexica knew: the sole textual citation in Böhtlingk's entry for nakṣatravṛkṣa is 'Rājan 2,41' (MW-3). (2) Nārada(-īya) Purāṇa, Pūrvabhāga 89.144–147, which carries the same 27 names in the same order (NARP-1 through NARP-4) — but EMBEDDED IN A DEVĪ NĀMĀVALI, in feminine epithet form, between the nakṣatra-deity series and the nakṣatra-yoni animal series. That it is the nakṣatra tree list is stated by the Motilal translation's own footnote (AITM-1) and supported by that edition's note that the immediately preceding series is the nakṣatra-deity list running Aśvinī to Pūṣan (AITM-3); the passage itself does not label the trees nakṣatra by nakṣatra. DATING: the Rājanighaṇṭu is placed in the 14th century by an aggregator page only (RDATE-1, RDATE-2), and the fetcher records that Meulenbeld could not be reached — treat the date as weakly sourced. For the Nārada Purāṇa, Hazra's early core is Pūrvabhāga chs. 1–41 and ch. 89 is OUTSIDE it (NDATE-1); Rocher holds the composition date of each Purāṇa unclear (NDATE-3); Wilson's low-end estimate is the 16th or 17th century (NDATE-4). NO SCHOLAR IN THIS LEDGER HAS COMPARED THE TWO PASSAGES OR STATED A PRIORITY, so this dossier states none (FRAMING §2.4). What can be said without inference is only this: Narahari's own verse names 'bṛhatsuśruta, nāradīya, nārāyaṇī' as the sources of the doctrine (RAJNI-6, ANAND-11), and a nāradīya text demonstrably carries it (NARP-1..4). The other two names he gives were searched for and not traced (see gaps).
whereTheModernVersionsDiverge: The Sanskrit witnesses agree closely on the NAMES; the modern circulating tables diverge from them mainly in the BOTANICAL IDENTIFICATION of ambiguous names, and in six cells they contradict the Sanskrit outright. Flat contradictions: Uttara Bhādrapadā, where every Sanskrit witness has nimba/ariṣṭa and the mirrored modern tables have a palm — Corypha umbraculifera (WIKI-6), tāla-druma (NRR-2); Hasta, where both Tier A witnesses have ambaṣṭha-taru and the modern tables offer Spondias, Azadirachta, Jasminum (WIKI-4), āmrāta (NRR-1) and Sapindus mukorossi (AW-2); Jyeṣṭhā, where three Sanskrit readings (śambara / saralā / mocā) meet at least four further modern ones (WIKI-5, CI-2, AW-3, BHAKTI-3, NRR-4); Ārdrā, where the main verse has kṛṣṇa and the modern tables have agarwood (CI-4, BHAKTI-4, WIKI-3), red sanders (SONI-4, AW-1) or ebony (WIKI-3) — one Wikipedia cell offering three mutually exclusive binomials at once (WIKI-3) and one astrology-portal row internally inconsistent, naming 'Black Eaglewood' and then printing the binomial for red sanders (AW-1); Anurādhā, where kesara / kakubhā / nāgapuṣpa meet 'Bakula, Nagkesa' offered together (CI-3) and Mimusops elengi (AW-4); Viśākhā, where both Tier A witnesses have vikaṅkata and the 1896 editor's variant list has babbulī (ANAND-8). PROVENANCE OF THE MODERN TABLES: the most widely mirrored one, the Wikipedia 'Nakshatravana' table, cites NO Sanskrit text anywhere on the page, and its only substantive reference is a 2012 newspaper article (WIKI-8) which the fetcher could not open (HTTP 403). The one peer-reviewed paper retrieved names no Sanskrit primary text for its nakṣatra table either (SONI-7). The practitioner lists name no source at all (CI-1). So the divergence is not between two documented recensions; it is between a narrow, citable textual tradition and a broad modern circulation whose own provenance is largely unestablished.

publicationConstraints: This dossier is NOT a filled table and must not be rendered as one. 27 rows carry a Sanskrit name with a Tier A locus; only 8 carry any botanical binomial, and every one of those binomials is Tier B or Tier C. A renderer that prints a binomial column with 19 blanks is showing the evidence correctly; a renderer that fills them is committing protocol C2's fabricated-completion error.

The tier field on each entry grades the SANSKRIT NAME AT THE POSITION, which is Tier A. It does not grade the botanical identification. The botanical field carries its own tier inline so that field and prose cannot disagree (protocol C4).
Do not merge these rows into any samidha or dhūpa table, and do not label them 'Vedic plants'. Three categories, three textual homes; see whatThisIs.

Nārada Purāṇa 1,90.172 / 185 / 215 is DESCRIBED here and NOT QUOTED, and must not be quoted downstream. It pairs a target slot (the enemy) with an operative homa sequence and falls under FRAMING §5 C-5. Its existence, locus and category are the publishable facts.
Carry no quantity, no preparation and no process parameter for any plant in this dossier (FRAMING §5 C-1, §11.2.1). None is recorded here and none may be added.

No efficacy claim. Rājanighaṇṭu 2.41 calls these trees āyuṣya-da and 2.45 asserts a penalty for medicinal use of one's own birth-star tree; both are recorded as WHAT THE TEXT SAYS, and the site asserts nothing about outcomes (FRAMING §1.1, §11.2.3).

entries.protectedStatus: PROTECTED ON EITHER MODERN READING, AND THE STATUS IS UNEVENLY VERIFIED. If the aguru/agarwood reading is taken: all agarwood-producing taxa are in CITES Appendix II, Aquilaria malaccensis listed 1994 and the rest of the genus subsequently (CITES-2), governed by annotation #14 agreed at CoP16 Bangkok 2013 (CITES-3), and the analysis notes wood chips traded for burning as incense wood (CITES-4). If the red sanders reading is taken: Soni et al. state in their own table that red chandan is endemic to India and considered worldwide endangered (SONI-5). CAVEAT ON THE EVIDENCE: the fetcher recorded that cites.org returned HTTP 403 on every route, so the Appendix-II status here rests on the IUCN/TRAFFIC CoP17 analysis and NOT on the official appendices, and the listings for Pterocarpus santalinus and Santalum album were NOT independently verified against CITES at all.

AMBIGUOUS INSIDE THE RĀJANIGHAṆṬU, AND THE AMBIGUITY IS RESOLVED DIFFERENTLY BY DIFFERENT LATER SOURCES. That text glosses vañjula as vetasa/nicula at 9.106 (RAJNI-12) and as aśoka at 10.53 (RAJNI-13) — a reed and a tree. The 1896 variant list reads vetra here (ANAND-9) and a commercial supplier reads jala-vetra (BHAKTI-3), i.e. both take the reed branch of the ambiguity. Both Tier A witnesses have vañjula; only the derivative sources choose.

Both Tier A witnesses read panasa; the 1896 editor's footnote reads nicula, which the Rājanighaṇṭu's own synonym verse at 9.106 puts in the vetasa/vañjula group (RAJNI-12) — i.e. the variant list appears to shift the reed one position, putting vetra at 20 and nicula at 21 where the main verse has vañjula at 20 and pānasa at 21. THAT SHIFT IS AN OBSERVATION ABOUT THE TWO LISTS AS THIS LEDGER RECORDS THEM, not a text-critical conclusion, and no scholar in the ledger has commented on it. The commercial supplier follows the main verse (BHAKTI-3).

Three Sanskrit witnesses, one name. THE MOST IMPORTANT SINGLE CELL FOR THE ANTI-CONFLATION ARGUMENT: arka is also the FIRST member of the samidh series in Atharvaveda-Pariśiṣṭa 26,5.6cd–5.7ab (AVP-7), and that text's very next words index that series to the grahas beginning with the Sun (AVP-8) — where arka is the Sun's own name. The same plant therefore sits at nakṣatra 22 in one system and at graha 1 in a different one. That is exactly the coincidence that makes the modern merge look plausible, and it is the reason the categories have to be kept apart by their INDEX, not by their contents. No toxicity assessment for arka appears anywhere in this ledger and none is asserted here.

Four sources, one name — the flattest agreement in the list. ANTI-CONFLATION CONTRAST: for the same nakṣatra under its older name Śraviṣṭhā, the Nakṣatrakalpa's BATHING rule prescribes sandalwood, not śamī (AVP-5). Two nakṣatra-indexed plant systems, two different plants at the same mansion — which is the cleanest single demonstration in this ledger that a nakṣatra-indexed plant is not automatically a nakṣatra-vṛkṣa.

Two of the three Sanskrit witnesses read kadamba; the Nārada Purāṇa reads halipriyā, and THIS LEDGER CONTAINS NO SYNONYM VERSE EQUATING THEM, so this dossier does not equate them, however conventional the equation is. The practitioner source that gives Kadamb for this position misnames the nakṣatra itself, printing 'Ghanitha' where Śatabhiṣā belongs (BHAKTI-5) — recorded because it is a fair sample of the care taken by the commercial layer.

contestedPoints: WHICH WITNESS IS EARLIER — UNSETTLED, AND THIS DOSSIER TAKES NO POSITION. The Rājanighaṇṭu is dated to the 14th century by a Tier C aggregator page only (RDATE-1, RDATE-2), with Meulenbeld — the standard authority on its date — unreachable, so the fetcher explicitly flags the date as weakly sourced. The Nārada Purāṇa's ch. 89 sits OUTSIDE Hazra's pre-11th-century core of Pūrvabhāga chs. 1–41 (NDATE-1); Rocher holds every Purāṇa's composition date unclear (NDATE-3); Wilson's low-end estimate for the text is the 16th or 17th century (NDATE-4), which would make it LATER than Narahari. No scholar in this ledger has compared the two passages or stated a priority, so under FRAMING §2.4 none is stated here. What is on the record without inference: Narahari names nāradīya among his sources (RAJNI-6, ANAND-11) and a nāradīya text carries the list (NARP-1..4).

WHETHER THE NĀRADA PURĀṆA PASSAGE IS A TREE LIST AT ALL, OR A NĀMĀVALI THAT LATER READERS INDEXED AS ONE. The 27 names occur as feminine epithets of the Goddess, between the nakṣatra-deity series and the nakṣatra-yoni animal series (NARP-1 through NARP-4); the passage does not label them nakṣatra by nakṣatra. The identification is made by the Motilal edition's footnote (AITM-1) and supported by its note that the preceding series is the nakṣatra-deity list from Aśvinī to Pūṣan (AITM-3) — i.e. it is an EDITORIAL identification, Tier B, resting on position. It is corroborated by the fact that the Rājanighaṇṭu's independently stated list (RAJNI-4) matches it name for name at most positions, and by the same Purāṇa using the term nakṣatra-vṛkṣa as a live category elsewhere (NARP-5, NARP-6, NARP-7). Both readings are kept.

THE 19TH-CENTURY LEXICOGRAPHERS KNEW ONLY ONE LOCUS. Monier-Williams defines nakṣatra-vṛkṣa as a tree consecrated to a nakṣatra (MW-1), Böhtlingk's shorter Wörterbuch the same (MW-2), and the sole textual citation the latter gives is 'Rājan 2,41' (MW-3). Whether that reflects the doctrine's actual textual distribution or only the lexicographers' reading is not settled by anything here — but it is direct evidence that the circulation of this list in modern practice is far wider than its documented textual footprint.

JYEṢṬHĀ (18) IS UNRESOLVABLE ON THIS EVIDENCE. Three Sanskrit readings — śambara, saralā, mocā (RAJNI-3, NARP-3, NAG-1, ANAND-8) — plus a threefold internal ambiguity in the Rājanighaṇṭu's own glosses of śambara as tāla, lodhra and arjuna (RAJNI-9, RAJNI-10, RAJNI-11), plus at least four further modern readings (BHAKTI-3, CI-2, AW-3, WIKI-5, NRR-4). Every position is kept and none is preferred.

ĀRDRĀ (6) — THE SANSKRIT SAYS kṛṣṇa, THE MODERN TABLES SAY AGARWOOD, AND THE BRIDGE IS AN 1896 EDITOR'S FOOTNOTE. Main-verse kṛṣṇa (RAJNI-2, ANAND-3) is glossed kāśmīra-vṛkṣa by the same text (RAJNI-14); the variant list reads aguru (ANAND-5); modern sources read agarwood (BHAKTI-4, CI-4), red sanders (SONI-4, AW-1) or ebony (WIKI-3). All positions kept. Both leading modern identifications carry protection concerns (CITES-2, SONI-5), and the CITES evidence itself is partial (see honestLimits).

ANURĀDHĀ (17) CARRIES A DIVERGENCE INSIDE A TRANSLATION AS WELL AS BETWEEN TEXTS. The printed Nag page image reads kakubhā (NAG-1) and the GRETIL text agrees (NARP-3), while the Motilal English prints 'Vakula' at that item (AITM-2) — a reading its own base text does not carry. Meanwhile the Rājanighaṇṭu's kesara is glossed bakula by that text's own nānārtha verse (RAJNI-9), and the 1896 variant list reads nāgapuṣpa (ANAND-8). A modern list simply prints both bakula and nāgakesara (CI-3).

UTTARA BHĀDRAPADĀ (26): nimba/ariṣṭa in all three Sanskrit witnesses (RAJNI-3, NARP-4, ANAND-10) against a palm in the two most-mirrored modern tables (WIKI-6, NRR-2). Nothing in the ledger explains the substitution.
HASTA (13): ambaṣṭha-taru in both Tier A witnesses (RAJNI-2, NARP-2) against jātī in the variant list (ANAND-7) and four incompatible modern identifications (WIKI-4, NRR-1, AW-2).

UTTARA ĀṢĀḌHĀ (21) AND PŪRVA ĀṢĀḌHĀ (20) MAY BE OFFSET BY ONE IN THE VARIANT LIST. The main verse reads vañjula at 20 and pānasa at 21 (RAJNI-3); the 1896 footnote reads vetra at 20 and nicula at 21 (ANAND-9), and the Rājanighaṇṭu's own gloss puts vetasa and nicula in the same synonym group (RAJNI-12). Whether that is a one-position shift or two independent variants is NOT determined by anything in this ledger and no scholar in it has commented.

WHETHER THE NAKṢATRA TREE IS A SAMIDHA. In the modern market it is sold as one (BHAKTI-1, BHAKTI-2). In the Atharvan material it plainly is not — that corpus indexes samidh by graha (AVP-7, AVP-8) and by purpose (AVP-9). But the Nārada Purāṇa itself burns a person's birth-nakṣatra tree as homa fuel three times in one chapter (NARP-5, NARP-6, NARP-7). So the categories are distinct in their indexing and NOT hermetically sealed in practice, and both halves of that are on the record here rather than resolved into whichever is tidier.

TEXT-CRITICAL RELIABILITY OF THE NĀRADA E-TEXT. The GRETIL file's own header warns that after many corrections the text still needs proof-reading (NARP-9), and it was input by the Sansknet project (NARP-8). Printed confirmation from page images exists in this ledger for v. 144 (NAG-2) and v. 146 (NAG-1) but NOT for v. 145 — for which the ledger holds only an archive.org OCR line, itself visibly corrupt (रोरिणा for रोहिणा) and covering only the first half of the verse (NAG-3). Nakṣatras 12–15 of the Nārada list are therefore unconfirmed against print in this ledger.

WHAT THE RĀJANIGHAṆṬU CLAIMS FOR THESE TREES, RECORDED AS THE TEXT'S CLAIM AND NOTHING MORE. Its opening verse calls them to be honoured and āyuṣya-da, and ties that to nurturing and protecting them (RAJNI-1, ANAND-2); v. 2.45 asserts that a mortal who, blind with pride, makes medicines from the tree of his OWN birth-star loses longevity, prosperity, wife and son (RAJNI-5). These are reported as statements the text makes. THE SITE ASSERTS NO EFFICACY AND NO OUTCOME OF ANY KIND (FRAMING §1.1, §1.5, §11.2.3), and carries no quantity and no preparation.
honestLimits: WHAT THIS DOSSIER ESTABLISHES: the 27-tree nakṣatra list is genuinely textually attested, at two loci, in Sanskrit, quotable and public-domain, and the Sanskrit name at each of the 27 positions can be cited to a text and a verse — with the Rājanighaṇṭu stating its own count and indexing rule in its own words (RAJNI-4) rather than requiring the reader to count. That is a stronger result than the round's brief anticipated. WHAT IT DOES NOT ESTABLISH, IN ORDER OF HOW MUCH IT MATTERS. (1) BOTANY. Nineteen of twenty-seven cells have NO botanical identification from any source in this ledger, and the eight that do are all Tier B or Tier C; no Tier A source identifies a single plant by binomial. A binomial column would be 70% fabrication. (2) DATE AND PRIORITY. Neither witness is securely dated and no scholar in this ledger has compared them, so 'the earliest text that carries the list' cannot be answered with one name — it is answered with two witnesses, their dating evidence, and a stated refusal to order them. The fetcher's own summary line calls the Nārada Purāṇa the earliest located witness; on the dating evidence in the same ledger (NDATE-1, NDATE-3, NDATE-4) that does not follow, and this dossier declines to carry it. (3) SYNONYM EQUATIONS. Where two witnesses give different Sanskrit names at the same position, this dossier equates them ONLY where a nānārtha verse in the ledger says so — which happens at exactly three positions (Aśvinī via RAJNI-8, Kṛttikā via RAJNI-7, Maghā via RAJNI-14). At Bharaṇī (dhātrī / āmalā), Puṣya (aśvattha / pippala), Punarvasu (vaṃśa / veṇu), Mūla (sarja / rāla), Śatabhiṣā (kadamba / halipriyā), Uttara Bhādrapadā (nimba / ariṣṭa) and Revatī (madhuka / mohavṛkṣa) the equations are conventional and probably right and ARE NOT MADE HERE, because making them without a sid is precisely the invented-attribution failure this protocol exists to stop. A reader who wants them made needs a nighaṇṭu the fetcher did not reach. (4) DEVANAGARI. The devanagari field is populated only where a ledger snippet carries the actual glyphs — which means the main verse for positions 1–13 (ANAND-3), the 1896 variant list for most positions, and the Nag page images for parts of the Nārada text. It is EMPTY for the main verse at positions 14–27 because the Ānandāśrama snippets stop at v. 34. Nothing was back-transliterated from IAST. (5) SCOPE OF THE NEGATIVE RESULTS. 'The Bṛhat Saṃhitā has no such list' is confirmed for chs. 15, 97 and 55, which is where it would be, not for a line-by-line read of all 106 chapters. The Matsya check covers adhyāyas 1–176 only. No Saṃhitā, Brāhmaṇa or Sūtra text was searched at all, so the widely repeated claim of an Atharvavedic root is neither supported nor refuted here — it is simply not looked at, and that is recorded as a gap rather than converted into an absence. (6) THE PROTECTED-SPECIES EVIDENCE IS PARTIAL. cites.org returned HTTP 403 on every route the fetcher tried, so agarwood's Appendix-II status rests on an IUCN/TRAFFIC CoP17 analysis rather than the official appendices, and the listings for Pterocarpus santalinus and Santalum album were never independently verified — only Soni et al.'s 'considered worldwide endangered' remark is on the record for red sanders. Any downstream page must carry that qualification with the flag. (7) ONE FETCHER GLOSS IS NOT EVIDENCE AND IS MARKED AS SUCH: the claim that śruva-vṛkṣa is a synonym of vikaṅkata appears in the ledger only inside a locus annotation (NRR-3), written by the fetcher, not stated by any source; it is reported here as the fetcher's gloss and not used as an identification. (8) FINALLY, THE COMPARATIVE MATERIAL IS ASYMMETRIC BY CONSTRUCTION. Six Tier C practitioner and commercial sources were fetched and two Tier B papers, against four Tier A Sanskrit texts. That is the right shape for the question asked — the point was to locate the textual floor under a very large modern circulation — but it means the modern-divergence findings rest on a convenience sample of what was reachable, and three of the modern sources most likely to carry a citation were unreachable behind HTTP 403.
